title: Logic & Critical Thinking
description: Separate fact from opinion, spot broken arguments, read risk properly, and make clearer decisions.

stations.title: Fact vs Opinion
stations.summary: Facts can be tested. Opinions can be debated. Many arguments collapse when the two are swapped.
points: A fact can be shown true or false with evidence ('Water boils at 100°C at 1 atm').
An opinion is a judgement or preference ('Nasi goreng is nicer than soto').
A claim demands evidence. The bigger the claim, the stronger the evidence needed.
Ask: 'What is the evidence?' and 'How could this be shown false?'

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fact?
options: Nasi goreng is better than mie goreng
Blue is the most beautiful colour
questions.explain: It can be measured with instruments and comes out the same for everyone.

questions.prompt: 'In my view, this rainy season is more annoying.' This is...
questions.explain: It contains a subjective judgement ('annoying', 'in my view'). Valid as an opinion, not a fact.

questions.prompt: The best way to check a claim is to...
options: Look for evidence and possible refutations
Count how many people like it
questions.explain: Critical thinking actively asks how a claim could be wrong, rather than only seeking confirmation.

stations.title: Common Fallacies
stations.summary: A fallacy is an argument that sounds convincing but is logically broken.
points: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument.
Bandwagon: 'everyone does it' does not make it right.
Straw man: twisting the other side's argument so it is easy to knock down.
False dilemma: pretending there are only two options when there are more.

questions.prompt: 'Your idea must be wrong because you are young.' This is...
questions.explain: The attack targets the person (age), not the substance of the argument.

questions.prompt: 'Millions of people use it, so it must be safe.' This is...
questions.explain: Popularity is not evidence of truth or safety (appeal to popularity).

questions.prompt: 'If we do not ban A, tomorrow disaster Z will surely happen.' This pattern is...
questions.explain: It chains extreme outcomes together without evidence for each step.

cards.back: Attacks the person, not the argument

stations.title: Probability & Risk
stations.summary: Human brains are built for stories, not percentages — which is why risk is so often misread.
points: Independent events have no memory: five heads in a row still leaves a 50% chance on the sixth toss.
Small risks repeated become large: 1% a year does not mean safe forever.
Compare with the base rate: 'cuts the risk by 50%' sounds huge if the starting risk was 2%.
Absolute risk is more meaningful than relative risk.

questions.prompt: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. The chance of heads on the sixth toss is...
questions.explain: Each toss is independent: the coin keeps no memory. Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy.

questions.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. The chance of an even number is...
questions.explain: Even faces: 2, 4, 6 → three out of six outcomes = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.prompt: 'This medicine cuts the risk by 50%.' The statement most needs...
questions.explain: A 50% relative cut from a 2% risk only brings it to 1% — an absolute difference of one point.

cards.back: No memory: the chance stays the same
The real difference, more useful than relative %

stations.title: Bias & Decisions
stations.summary: Nobody is fully objective. Knowing the name of a bias already weakens it.
points: Confirmation bias: only looking for information that supports what you already believe.
Sunk cost fallacy: continuing because of time or money already spent.
Anchoring: the first number you hear drags your later judgements towards it.
Practical antidotes: write the criteria before seeing the options, and ask someone who disagrees.

questions.prompt: Only reading news that agrees with you is called...
questions.explain: Feeds reinforce it too, so deliberately read sources that differ from you.

questions.prompt: 'The film is bad, but the ticket was expensive so I will watch it to the end.' This is...
questions.explain: Money already spent cannot return; only future benefit is relevant.

questions.prompt: The most practical way to reduce bias before choosing is to...
options: Write your criteria before looking at the options
Copy whoever is closest to you
questions.explain: Fixing criteria early stops your judgement being dragged around by later information.

cards.back: Seeking only evidence that supports existing beliefs
Continuing because of past cost, not future benefit
